item.title: Where Yurga Begins: XVII–XVIII Centuries
item.description:
Yurga is older than it seems.

Before the city, before the station, before the factories — there was a small Russian settlement called Ust-Iskitim. Late XVII century. Quiet life by the Tom River, surrounded by rivers, forests, and fertile banks.

The location was convenient: water nearby, a road along the river, good land. Back then, no one could imagine that in a couple of centuries, an industrial city known throughout Kuzbass would rise here.

item.title: First Mention of Yurga (1734)
item.description:
1734 — the first line about Yurga in a document.

During the Second Kamchatka Expedition, student S. P. Krasheninnikov traveled along the Tom River, carefully recording all settlements.

He described villages, rivers, and the distances between them — and among them, the word “Yurga” appeared for the first time. It was still referring to the river, but from this moment, the name entered the history of Siberia.

More than two hundred years have passed — and the names around are almost the same. It’s a very rare feeling: reading lines from the XVIII century and recognizing your own land.

item.title: Why Yurga is Called So: Versions
item.description:
The name “Yurga” is a mystery with several answers.

There were many versions:

  • Selkup — “fat river” (in spring the banks turned yellow from buttercups);
  • “pacer” or “small horse trot” — in Tatar interpretations;
  • and the most convincing modern version: Turkic origin, “fast river”.

Anyone who has seen Yurginka in spring understands: this name perfectly captures its character. Lively, noisy, “talkative” — the river gave its name to the place, and the place to the future city.

item.title: Old Yurga: First Houses and Settlers
item.description:
The first houses of Yurga were offshoots of the village of Polomoshnoye.

Approximately 1875–1876 (officially — 1886). People were drawn here by the fertile banks of the Yurga River.

The Berezovsky brothers — Alexander and Grigory — built the first houses. According to the 1901 census, there were about 40 residents. Few, but this was already the beginning of a real settlement.

Yurga grew quietly, like many Siberian settlements… until an event occurred nearby that would change its fate forever.

item.title: Trans-Siberian Railway: The Event That Changed Everything
item.description:
Without the railway, Yurga might have remained a village.

But the Trans-Siberian Railway passed nearby — and this became a turning point.

  1. The great road connects the country, and along with it changes the fates of cities. Yurga became part of this line — and from then on, its life was connected with rails, the station, and movement east and west.

The museum preserves a rail from that time — as a symbol of the point where a different scale began.

item.title: Birth of Yurga Station
item.description:
Yurga station opened in 1906.

But the siding plan was approved back in 1902: 4 tracks — main, passenger, passing, and military.

From 1906, Yurga became a railway settlement. Steam locomotives of series “O”, “S”, “U”, “E” worked here — reliable “workhorses” of the Siberian railways.

The station meant people, goods, movement. Yurga began to rapidly expand on both sides of the tracks.

Next — pre-revolutionary Yurga and station life.

item.title: Yurga Before the Revolution: Daily Life and Trade
item.description:
By 1910, Yurga station had everything needed for life.

A station building, military barracks, warehouses, merchants’ houses, a confectionery shop.

After Stolypin’s reform, settlers massively moved to Siberia. Yurga grew thanks to the land, the Tom River, and convenient trade via the Kuznetsk highway.

Pre-revolutionary streets had different names: Lenin Street was Pochtamtskaya, Kalinin Street was Yakovlevskaya… But the feeling of a small bustling settlement by the road was already urban.

item.title: 1917–1919: Soviet, Govorov, and the Civil War
item.description:
The Revolution in Yurga wasn’t stormy, but it was real.

In 1917, the Council of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies was established. Chairman — Alexey Grigoryevich Govorov, a carpenter from the railway.

The Soviet managed to accomplish much: 8-hour workday, school, medical clinic, help for the poor, Red Guard detachment.

But in 1918, the White Czechs crushed the Soviet. Govorov went through underground work, arrests, “death trains,” rescue by partisans… His family later survived repressions and war. A personal fate — like a mirror of the country.

item.title: 1920s–1930s: NEP, Collectivization, and Siblag
item.description:
The 1920s — Yurga learns to live anew.

Subbotniks, wagon repairs, help for starving Volga region, evening schools, libraries. Komsomol — the engine of new life.

NEP revives trade. Then comes collectivization: collective farms multiply, nearby are Siblag territories, camps, repressions of 1937.

Yurga — part of a large country, so its history during this period is just as sharp and difficult.

Next — about the decision to build a machine-building plant.

item.title: The Factory and the War: 1940–1945
item.description:
1940 — construction of the factory began.

And in 1941, evacuation trains arrived in Yurga: workers and equipment from Stalingrad, Leningrad, Moscow, Kramatorsk.

They built in barracks, without roads, in winter hands stuck to metal — but they launched the factory. February 6, 1943 — the machine-building plant was officially put into operation.

In June 1944, the first products were produced, tested at the proving ground, and sent to the front. Yurga became a worker city and a soldier city: 12 thousand went to the front, more than 5.5 thousand did not return.

item.title: Post-War Prosperity
item.description:
After the war, Yurga grew together with the factory.

City status: 1949 — city of district subordination, 1953 — regional.

The machine-building plant became a city-forming giant. In parallel, the trust “Yurgapromstroy” built: schools, cultural centers, cinema, medical facilities, sports complexes, residential quarters.

In the 1960s, large-panel construction boom begins, the city becomes modern. And in the 1960s, a second giant rises — the abrasive factory.

Series finale — about the crisis of the 90s and today’s character of the city.

item.title: The 90s and Beyond: Crisis, Survival, and Faith
item.description:
The 90s were hard on Yurga.

Barter, income stratification, privatization. And in 1994, the crisis hit the machine-building plant: wages weren’t paid for months, strikes began.

Some called the city dying. But Yurga did not die. People endured and preserved the city because they knew how to work and stick together — just as they once built the factory, as they survived the war.

Today Yurga lives in a new century with faith in itself. And this, perhaps, is the main idea of the entire history.

I actually enjoy this mix. Identity work brings together technical problem-solving, security, user experience, automation, and teamwork. A login may look like one small action, but making it feel that simple takes a surprising amount of thoughtful work behind the scenes.

item.title: Systems Administrator
item.description:
T3Leads is the world’s premier online lead generation firm and affiliate network. T3Leads’ expertise is in providing quality payday loan leads, as the go-to pay-per-lead affiliate network for the financial sector. With over 10,000 active affiliates, T3Leads currently operates in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia.

As a Senior Systems Administrator & Network Security Administrator at T3Leads, my responsibilities include: Network Security • Ensuring system security, spearheading security audits, and working with the Hi Level White Hackers team for penetration testing • Utilizing security tools to monitor the networks and reporting and responding immediately to security or usability issues and incidents • Writing custom monitoring plugins to ensure system security • Coordinating and installing patches and releases on web applications and development, pre production, and production systems • Diagnosing and resolving network connectivity interruptions, including malware infections, faulty hardware, and configuration issues • Implementing functional backup plans and disaster recovery plans • Scheduling, creating, and verifying backups on a regular and ad hoc basis • Deploying backup, antivirus, monitoring, blade logic, and asset management agents as servers are added into the network • Hands on experience with computer forensics, penetration and vulnerability testing tools, and conducting internal audits, vulnerability scanning, firewall, penetration testing • Install, diagnose, repair, and upgrade all hardware, applications and equipment, including regulation of any software incidents

From a terminal

No browser needed. The response is always just the plain IP address — nothing else — so it's safe to pipe straight into a script.

item.title: Password Generator
item.description:
Generate a password

Character types

How this actually works

  • Uses the Web Crypto API's crypto.getRandomValues() — a cryptographically secure random number generator, not Math.random(), which was never designed to be unpredictable.
  • Character selection uses rejection sampling to avoid modulo bias, a subtle mistake in many password generators that quietly makes some characters more likely to appear than others.
  • If you select more than one character type, one of each is guaranteed to appear — then the whole password, including where those guaranteed characters end up, is shuffled using the same secure randomness.
  • Nothing is sent anywhere. The password is generated and stays entirely in this browser tab — close or reload the page and it's gone for good.

From a terminal

These generate a password the same way this page does — locally, using your machine's own cryptographically secure random number generator — with nothing sent to any server. There's deliberately no curl-based option here, unlike the IP tool: a password generator that has to ask a server for the password isn't one where "nothing is sent anywhere" is actually true anymore.
